concepts.name: Sets
concepts.summary: Collections of distinct objects, and the membership relation on which the rest of mathematics is built.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: An assignment f: A → B giving each element of a domain A exactly one value in a codomain B.

concepts.name: Limits
concepts.summary: The value a function approaches as its input approaches a point — the idea that makes calculus rigorous.

concepts.name: Continuity
concepts.summary: A function is continuous where small changes in input produce small changes in output.

concepts.name: Derivatives
concepts.summary: The instantaneous rate of change of a function, defined as a limit of difference quotients.

concepts.name: Integrals
concepts.summary: The accumulation of a quantity over an interval, defined as a limit of Riemann sums.

concepts.name: Real Analysis
concepts.summary: The rigorous study of limits, continuity, differentiation and integration on the real line.

concepts.name: Complex Numbers
concepts.summary: Numbers of the form a + bi with i² = −1, forming an algebraically closed field.

concepts.name: The Unit Circle
concepts.summary: The circle of radius 1 centred at the origin, on which the trigonometric functions are defined geometrically.

concepts.name: Trigonometric Functions
concepts.summary: Sine and cosine as coordinates of a point moving on the unit circle.

concepts.name: Complex Exponentials
concepts.summary: The exponential function extended to complex arguments via its power series.

concepts.name: Euler's Formula
concepts.summary: e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x — the bridge between exponential and trigonometric functions.

timeline.text: Roger Cotes publishes a logarithmic form of the relation, without the exponential notation.
Euler states the formula in Introductio in analysin infinitorum and derives it from power series.
Wessel and later Argand give the geometric reading as rotation in the plane.

concepts.name: Periodic Functions
concepts.summary: Functions that repeat their values at regular intervals, f(x + T) = f(x).

concepts.name: Fourier Representation
concepts.summary: Any sufficiently well-behaved periodic function can be written as a sum of sines and cosines.

concepts.name: Fourier Analysis
concepts.summary: The study of how functions decompose into frequency components.

concepts.name: The Fourier Transform
concepts.summary: The integral transform carrying a function of time to a function of frequency.

concepts.name: Complex Analysis
concepts.summary: The study of differentiable functions of a complex variable, where differentiability is far more rigid than on the reals.

concepts.name: Analytic Continuation
concepts.summary: Extending a holomorphic function beyond its original domain while preserving analyticity; on a connected domain the extension is unique.

concepts.name: Polynomials
concepts.summary: Finite sums of powers of a variable with coefficients from a ring or field.

concepts.name: Groups
concepts.summary: A set with an associative operation, an identity, and inverses — the algebraic abstraction of symmetry.

concepts.name: Modular Arithmetic
concepts.summary: Arithmetic on remainders, where numbers wrap around after reaching a fixed modulus.

concepts.name: Prime Numbers
concepts.summary: Integers greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and themselves — the multiplicative atoms of the integers.

concepts.name: The Riemann Zeta Function
concepts.summary: ζ(s) = Σ n^{−s}, continued analytically to the whole complex plane except s = 1.

concepts.name: The Prime Counting Function
concepts.summary: π(x), the number of primes not exceeding x, and the question of how smoothly it grows.

concepts.name: Euclidean Geometry
concepts.summary: The geometry of flat space governed by Euclid’s five postulates.

concepts.name: Inner Product Spaces
concepts.summary: Vector spaces carrying a notion of angle and length, generalising the dot product.

concepts.name: Vector Fields
concepts.summary: An assignment of a vector to every point of a space — the objects that flow, circulate and diverge.

concepts.name: Differential Forms
concepts.summary: Objects built to be integrated over curves, surfaces and higher-dimensional regions.

concepts.name: Manifolds
concepts.summary: Spaces that look locally like Euclidean space, on which calculus can still be done.

concepts.name: Planar Graphs
concepts.summary: Graphs that can be drawn in the plane without edges crossing.

concepts.name: Probability Spaces
concepts.summary: A sample space, a σ-algebra of events, and a measure assigning each event a probability.

concepts.name: Random Variables
concepts.summary: Measurable functions from a probability space to the reals.

concepts.name: Conditional Probability
concepts.summary: The probability of one event given that another has occurred: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), defined whenever P(B) > 0.

concepts.name: Independence
concepts.summary: Events or variables whose joint behaviour factorises into their separate behaviours.

concepts.name: Expectation & Variance
concepts.summary: The mean of a random variable and the average squared spread about that mean.

concepts.name: The Normal Distribution
concepts.summary: The bell-shaped density determined entirely by its mean and variance.

concepts.name: Signal Processing
concepts.summary: Filtering, sampling and reconstructing signals — an engineering discipline resting on frequency decomposition.

concepts.name: Medical Imaging
concepts.summary: Reconstructing an interior image from exterior measurements, as in CT and MRI.

concepts.name: Audio Compression
concepts.summary: Discarding frequency components the ear cannot resolve, as in MP3 and AAC.

concepts.name: Quantum Mechanics
concepts.summary: Physical states as unit vectors in a complex Hilbert space, evolving under a one-parameter unitary group generated by the Hamiltonian.

concepts.name: Cryptography
concepts.summary: Protecting information using problems that are easy to state and hard to invert.

concepts.name: Statistical Inference
concepts.summary: Drawing conclusions about a population from a finite sample, with quantified uncertainty.

concepts.name: Machine Learning
concepts.summary: Fitting predictive models to data by optimising a loss function.

concepts.name: Computer Graphics
concepts.summary: Representing and rendering geometry, motion and light.

concepts.name: Satellite Navigation
concepts.summary: Locating a receiver by intersecting distance spheres from several satellites.

concepts.name: Euler's Identity
concepts.summary: e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, linking five fundamental constants in one equation.

timeline.text: Euler publishes the general formula from which the identity is the special case x = π.
The Argand-plane reading makes the identity a statement about a half-turn rotation.
Readers of the Mathematical Intelligencer vote it the most beautiful theorem in mathematics.

concepts.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
concepts.summary: For a continuous integrand, differentiation and integration are mutually inverse operations.

concepts.name: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
concepts.summary: Every non-constant complex polynomial has a complex root.

concepts.name: The Riemann Hypothesis
concepts.summary: All non-trivial zeros of the zeta function are conjectured to lie on the line Re(s) = ½.

concepts.name: Stokes' Theorem
concepts.summary: The integral of a form over a boundary equals the integral of its derivative over the region.

concepts.name: Bayes' Theorem
concepts.summary: How to update the probability of a hypothesis in the light of evidence.

concepts.name: The Central Limit Theorem
concepts.summary: Standardised sums of independent, identically distributed variables with finite non-zero variance converge in distribution to the standard normal.

concepts.name: The Pythagorean Theorem
concepts.summary: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c².

timeline.text: Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 lists Pythagorean triples.
The result is attributed to Pythagoras and his school.
Euclid gives a rigorous proof as Proposition I.47 of the Elements.

concepts.name: Fermat's Little Theorem
concepts.summary: For prime p and a not divisible by p, a^{p−1} ≡ 1 (mod p).

concepts.name: Euler's Polyhedron Formula
concepts.summary: For a convex polyhedron, V − E + F = 2.

concepts.name: The Gradient
concepts.summary: The vector of partial derivatives, pointing in the direction of steepest increase.

concepts.name: Divergence
concepts.summary: A scalar measure of how much a vector field spreads out from a point.

concepts.name: Curl
concepts.summary: A vector measure of how much a field circulates about a point.

concepts.name: Line Integrals
concepts.summary: Integration of a field along a curve — the work done moving through it.

concepts.name: Conservative Fields
concepts.summary: Fields that are gradients of a potential, where work depends only on the endpoints.

concepts.name: Vector Calculus
concepts.summary: The calculus of fields: gradient, divergence, curl and the theorems that link them.

concepts.name: Electromagnetism
concepts.summary: Maxwell’s equations state the divergence and curl of the electric and magnetic fields.

concepts.name: Fluid Dynamics
concepts.summary: Velocity fields whose divergence measures compression and whose curl measures vorticity.

concepts.name: Categories
concepts.summary: Objects together with composable arrows between them — structure described by relationships rather than elements.

concepts.name: Functors
concepts.summary: Structure-preserving maps between categories, carrying objects to objects and arrows to arrows.

concepts.name: Natural Transformations
concepts.summary: Maps between functors that commute with every arrow — the reason categories were invented.

concepts.name: Universal Properties
concepts.summary: Defining an object by what it does rather than what it is made of, up to unique isomorphism.

concepts.name: The Yoneda Lemma
concepts.summary: An object is completely determined by the arrows into it — knowing all relationships is knowing the thing.

concepts.name: Ordinary Differential Equations
concepts.summary: Equations relating a function of one variable to its derivatives.

concepts.name: Initial Value Problems
concepts.summary: An equation together with the data at one instant that picks out a single solution.

concepts.name: Linear Differential Equations
concepts.summary: Equations linear in the unknown and its derivatives; solutions of the homogeneous case form a vector space, so superposition applies.

concepts.name: Partial Differential Equations
concepts.summary: Equations relating a function of several variables to its partial derivatives.

concepts.name: The Heat Equation
concepts.summary: The prototype diffusion equation, and the problem Fourier invented his series to solve.

concepts.name: Dynamical Systems
concepts.summary: The long-run behaviour of solutions: equilibria, stability, periodic orbits and chaos.

concepts.name: Population Models
concepts.summary: Logistic and predator-prey equations describing how populations change over time.

concepts.name: Tangent Spaces
concepts.summary: The vector space of directions at a point of a manifold — the local linear model of a curved space.

concepts.name: Metric Tensors
concepts.summary: A smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space, giving a manifold its lengths and angles.

concepts.name: Riemannian Manifolds
concepts.summary: A smooth manifold carrying a positive-definite metric tensor — geometry without an ambient space.

concepts.name: Geodesics
concepts.summary: The straightest possible curves on a curved space, and locally the shortest.

concepts.name: Christoffel Symbols
concepts.summary: The derivatives of the metric, packaged so that differentiation makes sense on a curved space.

concepts.name: Curvature
concepts.summary: The failure of parallel transport to return a vector unchanged — how far a space bends.

concepts.name: General Relativity
concepts.summary: Gravity as the curvature of a spacetime metric, with matter telling space how to bend.

concepts.name: Vector Spaces
concepts.summary: A set closed under addition and scaling — the setting in which linearity makes sense.

concepts.name: Matrices
concepts.summary: Rectangular arrays of numbers that encode linear maps in a chosen basis.

concepts.name: Linear Maps
concepts.summary: Functions preserving addition and scaling — the structure-respecting maps of vector spaces.

concepts.name: Determinants
concepts.summary: A single number measuring how a linear map scales volume, and whether it is invertible.

concepts.name: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
concepts.summary: Non-zero vectors whose direction a linear map preserves, Av = λv, together with the scalars λ by which they are scaled.

concepts.name: Diagonalisation
concepts.summary: Rewriting a map in an eigenbasis, where it acts by simple independent scalings.

concepts.name: Singular Value Decomposition
concepts.summary: Every real matrix factors as A = UΣVᵀ with U, V orthogonal and Σ diagonal with non-negative entries — an orthogonal change of frame, a scaling along axes, and another.

concepts.name: Propositional Logic
concepts.summary: Statements combined with and, or, not and implies, and the truth tables that govern them.

concepts.name: Proof
concepts.summary: A finite chain of deductions from accepted premises to a conclusion.

concepts.name: Predicate Logic
concepts.summary: Logic with quantifiers, able to talk about all and some rather than single statements.

concepts.name: Axiomatic Systems
concepts.summary: A choice of undefined terms and unproved assumptions from which a theory is built.

concepts.name: Computability
concepts.summary: Which problems can be settled by an algorithm, and which provably cannot.

concepts.name: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems
concepts.summary: Any consistent, effectively axiomatised theory strong enough for elementary arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.

concepts.name: Floating-Point Arithmetic
concepts.summary: How real numbers are approximated in finite precision, and the rounding error that follows.

concepts.name: Newton’s Method
concepts.summary: Solving \(f(x)=0\) by repeatedly following the tangent line to the axis.

concepts.name: Interpolation
concepts.summary: Reconstructing a function between known sample points, usually with polynomials or splines.

concepts.name: Numerical Integration
concepts.summary: Estimating an integral from finitely many evaluations of the integrand.

concepts.name: Finite Differences
concepts.summary: Replacing derivatives by difference quotients so a differential equation becomes algebra.

concepts.name: Conditioning & Stability
concepts.summary: How much a problem amplifies input error, and whether an algorithm adds more of its own.

concepts.name: Counting Principles
concepts.summary: The sum and product rules — the two ways of counting a set of choices without listing them.

concepts.name: The Pigeonhole Principle
concepts.summary: If more objects than boxes are placed into boxes, some box holds at least two.

concepts.name: Permutations & Combinations
concepts.summary: Counting arrangements where order matters, and selections where it does not.

concepts.name: The Binomial Theorem
concepts.summary: The expansion of \((a+b)^n\) for a non-negative integer \(n\), whose coefficients count the \(k\)-element subsets of an \(n\)-element set.

concepts.name: Graph Theory
concepts.summary: The study of vertices joined by edges — connectivity, colouring, matching and flow.

concepts.name: Generating Functions
concepts.summary: Encoding a counting sequence as the coefficients of a formal power series.

concepts.name: Topological Spaces
concepts.summary: A set with a chosen family of open sets — the least structure in which continuity makes sense.

concepts.name: Homeomorphisms
concepts.summary: Continuous bijections with continuous inverse — when two spaces count as the same shape.

concepts.name: Connectedness
concepts.summary: A space that cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open pieces.

concepts.name: Compactness
concepts.summary: Every open cover has a finite subcover — the property that makes infinite arguments finite.

edges.why: A function is defined as a particular kind of relation between two sets — a subset of the Cartesian product in which every input appears exactly once. Without sets there is nothing for a function to map between.
A limit is a statement about the values a function takes near a point, so the function must be defined on a neighbourhood of that point before the limit can be asked about.
Continuity at a point is literally the statement that the limit of f as x → a exists and equals f(a). It is a limit condition, not an independent idea.
The derivative is defined as the limit of the difference quotient (f(x+h) − f(x))/h as h → 0. The whole content of differentiation is that this particular limit exists.
The Riemann integral is the limit of sums over partitions as the mesh goes to zero; existence of the integral is existence of that limit.
Continuity on a closed bounded interval is the standard sufficient condition for Riemann integrability, and it is what lets the accumulation function be differentiated later.
The theorem asserts that the accumulation function has a derivative, and that it equals the integrand. Half the statement is a derivative claim.
The theorem is about the integral of a derivative and the derivative of an integral, so the integral must already be defined for the statement to make sense.
Real analysis begins by asking exactly when the fundamental theorem holds: which functions are integrable, which derivatives are themselves integrable, and where the naive statement fails.

Complex analysis reuses the machinery of limits, convergence and uniform convergence from the real theory, then discovers that complex differentiability is a far stronger hypothesis than real differentiability.
The formula is an identity about e raised to an imaginary power, so the field in which i lives has to exist first, together with its arithmetic.
The identity is a statement in the complex field: it involves i as an exponent and asserts equality with the complex number 0.
The identity is exactly Euler’s formula evaluated at x = π: cos π = −1 and sin π = 0 give e^{iπ} = −1, and rearranging produces e^{iπ} + 1 = 0.
Substituting ix into the power series for the exponential and separating real and imaginary parts produces precisely the cosine and sine series — which is the proof of the formula.

The right-hand side of the formula is cos x + i sin x, so the trigonometric functions must be defined — and defined as functions of a real number, not of an angle in degrees — before the identity can be stated.
Sine and cosine are defined as the vertical and horizontal coordinates of a point travelling around the unit circle at unit speed; the circle is where their values come from.

The identity is the unit circle read algebraically: e^{iθ} traces the circle as θ runs over the reals, and θ = π is the half-turn that lands on −1. The equation and the picture are the same statement.
The identity is the single most-quoted value of the complex exponential, and it is the case that fixes the exponential’s period: e^{iθ} has period 2π precisely because e^{iπ} = −1.
Writing complex numbers as re^{iθ} turns multiplication into addition of angles, which is the computational basis of contour integration and the residue calculus.
Fourier analysis is built on the complex exponentials e^{inx}, whose orthogonality and periodicity are consequences of Euler’s relation.
e^{iθ} is periodic with period 2π, so it is the natural model of a pure oscillation — a periodic function with a single frequency and no other structure.
The Fourier series expands a periodic function in terms of other periodic functions; periodicity is what makes the expansion well posed on a bounded interval.
Fourier analysis is the study of when that representation converges, in what sense, and what the coefficients tell you about the original function.
Letting the period tend to infinity turns the discrete sum of Fourier coefficients into a continuous integral — the transform is the limiting case of the series.
The transform is defined by an integral against e^{−iωt}; convergence questions about that integral are exactly what makes the theory delicate.
The theorem is a statement about the roots of polynomials, so the objects and their degree must be defined before the claim can be made.
The theorem says the complex field is algebraically closed — it is a statement about ℂ, and it is false over ℝ, as x² + 1 shows.
The shortest proof of the theorem is complex-analytic: if a polynomial had no root, 1/p would be a bounded entire function and Liouville’s theorem would force it to be constant.
A group is a set carrying an operation, so the underlying collection has to exist before the structure can be imposed.
The integers mod n form a group under addition and, when n is prime, the non-zero residues form a group under multiplication — modular arithmetic is the first non-obvious example most students meet.
The theorem is stated as a congruence mod p; without the congruence relation there is no way to express it.
The result is false for composite moduli in general — primality is what makes the non-zero residues a group, which is what forces a^{p−1} ≡ 1.
The theorem is Lagrange’s theorem in disguise: the multiplicative group mod p has order p − 1, so every element’s order divides p − 1.
RSA decryption works because exponentiation mod n is invertible, and the exponent that inverts it is computed from Fermat’s theorem generalised by Euler’s totient.
Public-key schemes rely on operations that are cheap in one direction and expensive to reverse; modular exponentiation is the standard example.
π(x) counts primes, so the objects being counted must be defined first.
Euler’s product formula rewrites ζ(s) as a product over primes, which is why an analytic function of a complex variable knows anything about the integers at all.
The series Σ n^{−s} converges only for Re(s) > 1; everything interesting about ζ lives on the rest of the plane and requires complex-analytic tools to reach.
The zeros that the Riemann hypothesis is about lie in the critical strip, where the defining series diverges — they exist only on the continued function.
Uniqueness of the continuation follows from the identity theorem, which is a complex-analytic fact with no real-variable analogue.
The hypothesis is a statement about the location of the zeros of ζ, so the function and its continuation must exist before the conjecture can be posed.
The hypothesis is equivalent to a sharp error bound in the prime number theorem: π(x) = Li(x) + O(√x log x). The zeros control how far the primes stray from their average density.
Bounds on prime gaps that follow from the hypothesis underpin the running-time analysis of prime-generation algorithms used to produce cryptographic keys.
The theorem is a proposition of Euclidean geometry and fails in curved space; the parallel postulate is what makes it true.
The equation of the unit circle, x² + y² = 1, is the Pythagorean theorem applied to the radius — which is why cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.
The inner product is built so that ⟨v,v⟩ is the squared length; the Pythagorean relation becomes the statement that orthogonal vectors add in quadrature.
Fourier coefficients are inner products of the function with the basis exponentials; convergence of the series is a statement about an orthonormal basis of a function space.
A receiver solves for its position by intersecting spheres of known radius about each satellite, and the distance equation for those spheres is the Pythagorean relation in three dimensions.
Distance tests, normalisation of direction vectors and lighting calculations all reduce to computing √(x² + y² + z²).
The classical statement equates the circulation of a vector field around a closed curve with the flux of its curl through any surface the curve bounds.
The general theorem, ∫_∂M ω = ∫_M dω, is stated for forms; the gradient, curl and divergence theorems are the cases of degree 0, 1 and 2.
The theorem needs a region with a boundary and a consistent orientation, which is exactly the structure a manifold with boundary provides.
Both sides of the identity are integrals; the theorem is a statement about when integration and differentiation can be traded against each other in higher dimensions.
The fundamental theorem of calculus is Stokes’ theorem in one dimension: the boundary of the interval [a,b] is the two points a and b, and ∫_a^b f′ = f(b) − f(a) is ∫_∂M ω = ∫_M dω.
Configuration spaces of constrained physical systems are manifolds, and the phase conventions of quantum states are described by bundles over them.
The standard proof projects the polyhedron onto the plane to get a connected planar graph, then removes edges one at a time; V − E + F is invariant under each removal.
V − E + F = 2 is the first appearance of the Euler characteristic, a topological invariant that classifies surfaces: 2 for the sphere, 0 for the torus.
The formula constrains which regular polyhedra can exist: solving V − E + F = 2 for regular faces meeting regularly at each vertex yields exactly the five Platonic solids.
Events are sets, and the axioms of probability are stated for a σ-algebra of subsets of the sample space.
A random variable is a measurable function on a probability space, so the space and its σ-algebra come first.
Conditioning restricts the sample space to B and renormalises the measure; it is an operation on a probability space, not a new axiom.
The theorem is an immediate rearrangement of the definition: both P(A|B)P(B) and P(B|A)P(A) equal P(A∩B), so the two conditionals determine each other.
Independence is the case where conditioning changes nothing: P(A|B) = P(A), equivalently P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).
Expectation is the integral of a random variable against the probability measure, so the variable must be defined and measurable first.
The normal distribution is parameterised entirely by its mean and variance, so both moments must be defined for the family to be described.
For a continuous random variable the expectation is ∫ x f(x) dx; the integral is what makes an average over a continuum meaningful.
The theorem’s hypothesis is that the summands are independent — without it the fluctuations can reinforce and the limit fails.
The statement is about the standardised sum (S_n − nμ)/(σ√n), so finite mean and variance are needed even to write it down.
The normal law is the limit the theorem identifies; it has to be defined before the convergence can be stated.
Confidence intervals and z-tests use the normal approximation to the sampling distribution of the mean, which is exactly what the theorem licenses for large samples.
Naive Bayes classifiers, Bayesian networks and posterior inference all compute P(hypothesis | data) from P(data | hypothesis) by the theorem.
Bayesian inference treats parameters as random and updates a prior into a posterior; the update rule is the theorem.
Iterative reconstruction algorithms treat the image as an unknown to be estimated from noisy projections, maximising a posterior probability.
The theorem explains why the normal distribution is ubiquitous in practice: any quantity that is the accumulation of many small independent effects inherits it.
Filtering is multiplication in the frequency domain: transform the signal, scale the components you want to keep or suppress, transform back.
An MRI scanner measures samples of the Fourier transform of the tissue directly; the image is produced by inverting the transform.
MP3 encoding transforms short windows of audio into frequency components and discards those a listener cannot perceive, which is only possible in the frequency representation.
Position and momentum wavefunctions are Fourier transforms of one another, and the uncertainty principle is the statement that a function and its transform cannot both be sharply localised.
The time evolution of a stationary state is multiplication by the phase e^{−iEt/ħ}; the periodicity of that phase — and hence energy quantisation on closed systems — is Euler’s relation at work.

Representing a sinusoid as the real part of a complex exponential turns tedious trigonometric identities into ordinary algebra with exponents, which is how phase and amplitude are handled in practice.
Linear models score an example by an inner product with a weight vector, and kernel methods replace that product with an inner product in a higher-dimensional space.
Training minimises a loss by gradient descent; backpropagation is the chain rule applied to a composition of many functions.
The theorem is what makes differentiation practically useful in reverse: to integrate a function you look for something whose derivative it is.
The gradient is the vector whose entries are the partial derivatives, so ordinary differentiation has to come first — one variable at a time, holding the others fixed.
Divergence is an operation applied to a field: it needs a vector assigned to every point before it can ask how much is flowing away from one.
Curl measures circulation of a field around a point, so the field itself must be defined on a neighbourhood of that point.
The gradient of a scalar function is the first vector field most students meet, and the model for every later one.
A line integral is an ordinary integral once the curve is parameterised — the parameter becomes the variable of integration.
The integrand is the field evaluated along the curve, dotted with the tangent, so the field has to exist along that path.
A field is conservative exactly when it is the gradient of some potential function; the definition is stated in terms of the gradient.
The defining property is about line integrals: in a conservative field the integral between two points is the same along every path.
Divergence is one of the three operators the subject is built from.
Curl is the second of the three operators, and the one that makes Stokes’ theorem possible.
The left-hand side of the classical statement is a line integral around the boundary curve.
The right-hand side is the flux of the curl through the surface, so curl must be defined before the theorem can be stated.

Both are first-order derivatives of a field, and they are complementary: divergence sees the part that spreads, curl sees the part that rotates. A field is determined by the two together, up to a harmonic remainder.
Maxwell’s four equations are statements about the divergence and curl of E and B; the whole theory is written in this language.
An incompressible flow is exactly one with zero divergence — nothing accumulates anywhere in the fluid.
Vorticity is the curl of the velocity field; it is what makes a whirlpool measurable.
A category generalises the pattern of sets and functions, so you need that concrete example before the abstraction means anything.
A group is exactly a category with one object in which every arrow is invertible — the definitions meet at a single example.
A functor is a map between categories, so both source and target have to exist first.
A natural transformation compares two functors, so it cannot be stated until functors are defined.
A universal property characterises an object by the arrows into or out of it, which presupposes the arrows of a category.
Yoneda is a statement about natural transformations out of representable functors; it is literally a theorem about them.
A differential equation is a relation among derivatives, so differentiation has to be in place before one can be written down.
An initial value problem is an equation plus a condition; the equation comes first.
Linear equations are the special case where solutions superpose, so the general notion is needed first.
The solution set of a homogeneous linear equation is a vector space; superposition is that structure in disguise.
Partial differential equations generalise ordinary ones to several independent variables.
The heat equation is a particular second-order partial differential equation.
Fourier introduced his series precisely to solve the heat equation by separating variables.
A dynamical system is what you study once you stop solving an equation and start asking how its solutions behave.
Logistic and predator-prey models are ordinary differential equations fitted to biological data.
A tangent space is attached to a point of a manifold, so the manifold has to come first.
The tangent space at a point is a vector space; its whole purpose is to be the local linear model.
A metric assigns an inner product to each tangent space, so there must be tangent spaces to equip.
A metric tensor is an inner product that varies smoothly from point to point — the pointwise notion is the building block.
A Riemannian manifold is by definition a manifold together with a positive-definite metric tensor.
The Christoffel symbols are built directly from first derivatives of the metric; without a metric there is nothing to differentiate.
The geodesic equation is written in terms of the Christoffel symbols, which supply the correction that makes acceleration meaningful on a curved space.
The Riemann tensor is assembled from the Christoffel symbols and their derivatives.
In general relativity the gravitational field is the spacetime metric; Einstein’s equations are a condition on its curvature.
Satellite clocks are corrected using the relativistic metric of spacetime; ignoring it puts positions out by kilometres per day.
A vector space is a set with extra operations, so the notion of a set underlies it.
Linear maps go between vector spaces; the spaces have to be defined before the maps between them.
A matrix is what a linear map looks like once a basis is chosen — the map is the object, the matrix is the notation.
The determinant is computed from the entries of a square matrix.
Eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\), which is a determinant condition.
Diagonalising a matrix means choosing a basis of its eigenvectors, so the eigenvectors must be found first.
The singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^{T}A\), so the eigenvalue problem sits underneath.
An inner product is extra structure placed on a vector space; the space comes first.
Principal component analysis is the singular value decomposition of a centred data matrix.
Rotations, scalings and projections of a scene are all matrix multiplications applied to coordinates.
Predicate logic adds quantifiers to the connectives of propositional logic, so the connectives come first.
A proof is a chain of inferences, and the inference rules are stated in terms of the connectives.
Axioms are sentences in a formal language, and predicate logic supplies that language.
Incompleteness is a statement about what a consistent axiom system can and cannot prove.
Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory is the axiom system most of mathematics is officially built on.
Decidability asks whether an algorithm can settle every sentence of a formal theory.
The halting problem and incompleteness are two faces of the same diagonal argument.
Security proofs reduce breaking a scheme to solving a problem believed to be hard.
Conditioning measures how rounding error already present in the input is amplified, so the model of rounding comes first.
Newton’s method steps along the tangent line, which is the derivative evaluated at the current guess.
The classical interpolant is the unique polynomial of least degree through the sample points.
Quadrature approximates the integral, so the exact object being approximated has to be defined.
Most quadrature rules integrate an interpolant exactly: fit a polynomial, then integrate that.
A finite difference is the difference quotient whose limit defines the derivative, stopped short of the limit.
Discretising the derivatives of a partial differential equation turns it into a large system of algebraic equations.
Ill-conditioned design matrices make fitted coefficients wildly sensitive to noise, which is why regularisation is used.
Counting is counting the elements of a set, so the language of sets comes first.
Permutations and combinations are the product rule applied to ordered and unordered selections.
The pigeonhole principle is a counting argument: it compares the size of two finite sets.
The binomial coefficients in the expansion are exactly the counts of \(k\)-element subsets.
Classical probability divides favourable arrangements by total arrangements, so both are counted the same way.
Graph arguments count vertices, edges, walks and colourings before anything else.
A planar graph is a graph with an extra drawing condition, so the general notion is needed first.
A generating function is a power series whose coefficients count; the binomial series is the first example.
A topology is a distinguished family of subsets, so the set and its subsets come first.
A homeomorphism is a map between topological spaces, which must therefore be defined.
Connectedness is stated in terms of open sets, which is exactly what a topology supplies.
Compactness is a condition on open covers, so the open sets have to be fixed first.
The open-set definition of a topology was reverse-engineered so that continuity could be stated without distances.
Extreme and intermediate value theorems on a closed interval are compactness and connectedness arguments in disguise.
A manifold is a space that is locally homeomorphic to Euclidean space, so the notion of homeomorphism is part of the definition.
The definite integral is defined as a limit of Riemann sums as the mesh of the partition tends to zero; without limits the definition cannot be stated.
Events are subsets of the sample space and a sigma-algebra is a family of such subsets, so set operations are the language probability is written in.
Eigenvalues are the roots of det(A - lambda I), so the determinant is what converts the eigenvector equation into a polynomial condition.
Independence is defined by P(A|B) = P(A), or equivalently by the product rule, so conditioning has to be defined first.
Arithmetic modulo n behaves like a field exactly when n is prime, which is why primality governs which congruences can be divided through.
A random variable is a function from the sample space to the reals, subject to a measurability condition; it is a function first.

articles.title: Divergence
articles.author: Dr. L. Vantongeren
articles.abstract: The divergence of a vector field measures the rate at which it spreads out from a point — positive at a source, negative at a sink, zero where nothing accumulates.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body:
For a field \(\mathbf{F}=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\) the divergence is the scalar

\[ \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial z} \]

It takes a vector field and returns a number at each point.

sections.heading: Derivation from flux
sections.body: Take a small box around a point and add up the outward flux through its six faces. Dividing by the volume and letting the box shrink gives exactly the sum of partial derivatives above — which is why divergence is often defined as flux per unit volume.

sections.heading: Reading the sign
sections.body: Positive divergence marks a source, negative a sink, and zero an incompressible flow. For the radial field \(\mathbf{F}=(x,y,z)\) the divergence is \(3\) everywhere: the field spreads uniformly.

references: Marsden, J.E. and Tromba, A. Vector Calculus. W.H. Freeman, 2011.
Schey, H.M. Div, Grad, Curl, and All That. Norton, 2004.

figure.caption: The potential whose gradient is the radial field. Drag to rotate: the surface rises away from the origin in every direction, which is what positive divergence looks like.

articles.title: Vector Fields
articles.author: R. Fennimore
articles.abstract: A vector field assigns a vector to every point of a region — a wind map, a flow, a force. It is the object on which gradient, divergence and curl all act.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body: A vector field on \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a function \(\mathbf{F}:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\). Where a scalar function gives a number at each point, a vector field gives a direction and a magnitude.

sections.heading: Examples
sections.body: The gradient \(\nabla f\) of any scalar function; the velocity of a fluid; the gravitational field \(\mathbf{F}=-\frac{GMm}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf{r}}\). Drawing a short arrow at each of a grid of points is the standard picture.

references: Marsden, J.E. and Tromba, A. Vector Calculus. W.H. Freeman, 2011.

articles.title: Euler's Identity
articles.author: Dr. E. Marchetti
articles.abstract: Euler's identity links five of the most important constants in mathematics — \(0\), \(1\), \(e\), \(i\), and \(\pi\) — in a single equation, and is frequently cited as an example of deep mathematical beauty.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
For the base of the natural logarithm \(e\), the imaginary unit \(i\), and \(\pi\), the identity states:

\[ e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0 \]

The equation combines addition, multiplication, exponentiation, and equality, alongside five fundamental constants, in a single compact statement.

sections.heading: Derivation from Euler’s Formula
sections.body:
Euler's identity follows directly from Euler's formula, which holds for any real number \(x\):

\[ e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x \]

Setting \(x = \pi\) gives \(e^{i\pi} = \cos\pi + i\sin\pi = -1 + i\cdot 0 = -1\), and rearranging yields \(e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0\).

sections.heading: Significance
sections.body: Beyond its aesthetic appeal, the identity is a special case of a broader correspondence between exponential and trigonometric functions that underlies Fourier analysis, AC circuit theory, and quantum mechanics.

references: Euler, L. Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748).
Nahin, P.J. Dr. Euler’s Fabulous Formula. Princeton University Press, 2006.

articles.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
articles.author: Dr. N. Osei
articles.abstract: The Riemann Hypothesis proposes that every non-trivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part \(\tfrac{1}{2}\). First conjectured in 1859, it remains one of the most consequential open problems in mathematics.

sections.heading: The Zeta Function
sections.body:
For a complex number \(s\) with real part greater than \(1\):

\[ \zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s} \]

The series converges only for \(\mathrm{Re}(s) > 1\). Riemann showed that \(\zeta\) extends uniquely by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on \(\mathbb{C}\), holomorphic everywhere except for a simple pole at \(s=1\) with residue \(1\).

sections.heading: Statement of the Hypothesis
sections.body:
The Riemann Hypothesis asserts that every non-trivial zero \(s\) satisfies:

\[ \mathrm{Re}(s) = \frac{1}{2} \]

Extensive numerical verification has confirmed this for trillions of zeros, though no general proof is known.

sections.heading: Status and Significance
sections.body: The hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems named by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. A resolution would sharpen our understanding of the distribution of prime numbers.

references: Riemann, B. Über die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse (1859).
Bombieri, E. Problems of the Millennium: The Riemann Hypothesis. Clay Mathematics Institute, 2000.

articles.title: Stokes' Theorem
articles.author: Dr. L. Vantongeren
articles.abstract: The generalized Stokes' theorem relates the integral of a differential form over the boundary of an oriented manifold to the integral of its exterior derivative over the manifold itself.

sections.heading: General Statement
sections.body:
Let \(M\) be a compact, oriented \(k\)-dimensional manifold with boundary \(\partial M\), and \(\omega\) a smooth \((k-1)\)-form on \(M\):

\[ \int_M d\omega = \int_{\partial M} \omega \]

sections.heading: Classical Special Cases
sections.body: In the plane this reduces to Green's theorem; on a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) it recovers the classical Kelvin–Stokes theorem; on a solid region it becomes the divergence theorem.

sections.heading: Significance
sections.body: Stokes' theorem is a foundational tool in differential topology and mathematical physics, including the formulation of Maxwell's equations in differential-forms language.

references: Spivak, M. Calculus on Manifolds. Addison-Wesley, 1965.
Lee, J.M. Introduction to Smooth Manifolds. Springer, 2013.

articles.title: Bayes' Theorem
articles.author: Dr. S. Iyer
articles.abstract: Bayes' theorem describes how to update the probability of a hypothesis in light of new evidence. It is the foundation of Bayesian inference, used across statistics, machine learning, and the sciences.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
For two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B) \neq 0\):

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)} \]

sections.heading: Derivation
sections.body: Since \(P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)\), solving for \(P(A \mid B)\) gives the theorem.

sections.heading: Worked example: a diagnostic test
sections.body:
Let \(D\) be the event that a person has a disease and \(+\) the event that they test positive. Suppose

\[ P(D)=0.01, \quad P(+\mid D)=0.99, \quad P(+\mid D^{c})=0.05 \]

so the prevalence is \(1\%\), the test detects \(99\%\) of true cases, and it returns a false positive for \(5\%\) of healthy people. The denominator comes from the law of total probability:

\[ P(+) = P(+\mid D)P(D) + P(+\mid D^{c})P(D^{c}) = (0.99)(0.01) + (0.05)(0.99) = 0.0594 \]

Therefore

\[ P(D \mid +) = \frac{(0.99)(0.01)}{0.0594} = \frac{0.0099}{0.0594} = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167 \]

A positive result raises the probability from \(1\%\) to about \(17\%\) — a large relative increase, but still far from certainty. The reason is that healthy people outnumber sick ones so heavily that their \(5\%\) false-positive rate produces five times as many positives as the disease itself. Reading \(P(+\mid D)=0.99\) as though it were \(P(D\mid +)\) is the base-rate fallacy.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.body: Bayes' theorem underlies spam filtering, medical diagnostic testing, and modern machine learning methods such as Bayesian networks and naive Bayes classifiers.

references: Bayes, T. An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances (1763).
Gelman, A. et al. Bayesian Data Analysis. CRC Press, 2013.

articles.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
articles.author: R. Fennimore
articles.abstract: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one complex root, guaranteeing that the complex numbers are algebraically complete.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body: For any non-constant polynomial \(p(z) = a_n z^n + \cdots + a_0\) with \(a_i \in \mathbb{C}\), there exists \(z_0\) such that \(p(z_0)=0\).

references: Gauss, C.F. Demonstratio nova theorematis (1799).

articles.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
articles.author: Dr. E. Marchetti
articles.abstract: For a continuous integrand, differentiation and integration are mutually inverse: the derivative of an accumulation function recovers the integrand, and a definite integral can be evaluated from any antiderivative.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\).

First part. Define \(F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\). Then \(F\) is differentiable on \((a,b)\) and \(F'(x)=f(x)\) there.

Second part. If \(G\) is any antiderivative of \(f\) on \([a,b]\), meaning \(G'=f\) throughout, then

\[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b)-G(a) \]

Continuity is doing the work in the first part: without it \(F\) need not be differentiable at every point. The second part holds more generally for any Riemann-integrable \(f\) admitting an antiderivative on \([a,b]\).

references: Newton, I. Method of Fluxions (1671, published 1736).

articles.title: The Pythagorean Theorem
articles.author: Dr. L. Vantongeren
articles.abstract: In a right triangle in the Euclidean plane, the square of the length of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
Let a triangle in the Euclidean plane have legs of length \(a\) and \(b\) meeting at a right angle, with hypotenuse of length \(c\). Then

\[ a^2+b^2=c^2 \]

The converse holds as well: if the three side lengths of a triangle satisfy \(a^2+b^2=c^2\), then the angle opposite the side of length \(c\) is a right angle (Euclid, Elements I.48). Both directions are theorems of Euclidean geometry and fail on the sphere and in the hyperbolic plane, where the angle sum of a triangle is not \(\pi\).

references: Euclid. Elements, Book I, Proposition 47 (c. 300 BC).

articles.title: Fermat's Little Theorem
articles.author: Dr. N. Osei
articles.abstract: If \(p\) is prime, then for any integer \(a\) not divisible by \(p\), \(a^{p-1}\equiv 1 \pmod p\).

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
Let \(p\) be prime and let \(a\) be an integer with \(p \nmid a\). Then

\[ a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p} \]

Multiplying through by \(a\) removes the hypothesis and gives the equivalent form \(a^{p} \equiv a \pmod p\), which holds for every integer \(a\). The converse fails: there are composite \(n\) with \(a^{n-1}\equiv 1 \pmod n\) for every \(a\) coprime to \(n\). These are the Carmichael numbers, the smallest being \(561 = 3 \times 11 \times 17\).

references: Fermat, P. Letter to Frénicle de Bessy (1640).

figure.caption: The standard normal density φ(x) = e^{-x²/2}/√(2π) — the limiting shape the theorem guarantees, whatever the distribution of the individual terms.

articles.title: The Central Limit Theorem
articles.author: Dr. S. Iyer
articles.abstract: If \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are independent and identically distributed with finite mean \(\mu\) and finite non-zero variance \(\sigma^2\), their standardised partial sums converge in distribution to the standard normal law, whatever the shape of the common distribution.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be independent and identically distributed with \(\mathbb{E}[X_i]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2\), where \(0 < \sigma^2 < \infty\). Then

\[ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \ \xrightarrow{d}\ \mathcal{N}(0,1) \]

The finite-variance hypothesis is not decorative. A Cauchy distribution has no finite mean or variance, and the average of \(n\) independent Cauchy variables is Cauchy again for every \(n\) — it never approaches a normal law. Note also that convergence is in distribution; the theorem says nothing about any individual realisation.

references: Lindeberg, J.W. Eine neue Herleitung des Exponentialgesetzes (1922).

articles.title: Euler's Polyhedron Formula
articles.author: Dr. T. Nakashima
articles.abstract: For any convex polyhedron, the numbers of vertices, edges, and faces are related by a strikingly simple formula.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.body:
For a convex polyhedron with \(V\) vertices, \(E\) edges and \(F\) faces:

\[ V - E + F = 2 \]

The convexity hypothesis matters; what is really required is that the surface be topologically a sphere. The quantity \(V-E+F\) is the Euler characteristic of the surface, and it takes other values otherwise — a polyhedron with a hole through it is topologically a torus and gives \(V-E+F=0\). Checking the cube: \(V=8\), \(E=12\), \(F=6\), so \(8-12+6=2\).

references: Euler, L. Elementa doctrinae solidorum (1758).

articles.title: Metric Tensors
articles.author: Dr. L. Vantongeren
articles.abstract: A metric tensor is a smoothly varying inner product on the tangent spaces of a manifold. It is the structure that turns a space with no notion of size into one with lengths, angles, areas and geodesics, and it is the object whose curvature describes gravity in general relativity.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body:
Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. A metric tensor \(g\) assigns to each point \(p \in M\) a bilinear form on the tangent space at that point:

\[ g_p : T_pM \times T_pM \to \mathbb{R} \]

subject to three conditions. It is symmetric, \(g_p(u,v) = g_p(v,u)\); it is non-degenerate, so that \(g_p(u,v)=0\) for every \(v\) forces \(u=0\); and it varies smoothly with \(p\). If in addition \(g_p(v,v) > 0\) for every non-zero \(v\), the metric is called Riemannian, and the pair \((M,g)\) is a Riemannian manifold.

Nothing here refers to a surrounding space. This is the essential point: the metric is intrinsic structure, so a surface knows its own geometry without being embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

sections.heading: Components and the Line Element
sections.body:
In a coordinate chart \((x^1,\dots,x^n)\) the metric is recorded by its components

\[ g_{ij} = g\!\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^i}, \frac{\partial}{\partial x^j}\right) \]

a symmetric \(n \times n\) matrix of functions. Applied to two tangent vectors \(u = u^i\partial_i\) and \(v = v^j\partial_j\), summation over repeated indices gives \(g(u,v) = g_{ij}u^i v^j\).

The same data is usually written as the line element, the squared length of an infinitesimal displacement:

\[ ds^2 = g_{ij}\,dx^i dx^j \]

This is the form in which a metric is almost always quoted, because reading off \(g_{ij}\) from it is immediate.

sections.heading: Example: the Plane in Two Coordinate Systems
sections.body:
In Cartesian coordinates on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) the metric is the identity matrix and \(ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2\), which is the Pythagorean theorem written infinitesimally.

Substituting \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\) gives the same geometry in polar coordinates:

\[ ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2\,d\theta^2, \qquad g_{ij} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & r^2 \end{pmatrix} \]

The components now depend on position, yet the plane is still flat. This is the standard warning: varying components do not mean curvature. They may only mean that the coordinates are curved. Distinguishing the two is precisely what the curvature tensor is for.

sections.heading: Example: the Round Sphere
sections.body:
On a sphere of radius \(R\), parametrised by colatitude \(\theta\) and longitude \(\varphi\),

\[ ds^2 = R^2\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\!\theta\, d\varphi^2\right) \]

The factor \(\sin^2\theta\) records that circles of constant latitude shrink towards the poles: a step of \(d\varphi\) covers less distance near the pole than at the equator. Unlike the polar plane above, no change of coordinates can reduce this metric to the identity anywhere on an open set — the sphere is genuinely curved, which is why every flat map of the Earth distorts something.

sections.heading: Lengths, Angles and Volume
sections.body:
Once a metric is fixed, the basic measurements of geometry follow. The length of a curve \(\gamma:[a,b] \to M\) is

\[ L(\gamma) = \int_a^b \sqrt{g_{ij}\,\dot\gamma^i\dot\gamma^j}\; dt \]

the angle \(\alpha\) between tangent vectors \(u\) and \(v\) satisfies

\[ \cos\alpha = \frac{g(u,v)}{\sqrt{g(u,u)}\,\sqrt{g(v,v)}} \]

and the volume element is \(dV = \sqrt{|\det g|}\; dx^1\cdots dx^n\). The determinant appearing here is why the Jacobian factor \(r\) shows up when integrating in polar coordinates: \(\sqrt{\det g} = \sqrt{1 \cdot r^2} = r\).

sections.heading: Raising and Lowering Indices
sections.body:
Non-degeneracy means the matrix \(g_{ij}\) is invertible; its inverse is written \(g^{ij}\), so that \(g^{ik}g_{kj} = \delta^i_j\). This gives a canonical isomorphism between tangent and cotangent spaces, used constantly in practice:

\[ v_i = g_{ij}v^j, \qquad v^i = g^{ij}v_j \]

Physicists call this lowering and raising indices. It is the reason the gradient of a function, which is naturally a covector \(\partial_i f\), can be treated as a vector \(g^{ij}\partial_j f\) pointing in the direction of steepest ascent. Without a metric there is no such correspondence.

sections.heading: From the Metric to Curvature
sections.body:
The metric determines a unique torsion-free connection compatible with it, the Levi-Civita connection, whose coefficients are the Christoffel symbols

\[ \Gamma^{k}_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{2} g^{kl}\left(\partial_i g_{jl} + \partial_j g_{il} - \partial_l g_{ij}\right) \]

These are built from the metric alone, and from them the Riemann curvature tensor \(R^{\rho}_{\ \sigma\mu\nu}\) is assembled. Geodesics — the straightest available curves — satisfy \(\ddot x^k + \Gamma^k_{ij}\dot x^i \dot x^j = 0\).

So the whole chain runs in one direction: choose a metric, and the connection, the geodesics and the curvature are all determined. This is the sense in which the metric is the fundamental object of Riemannian geometry.

sections.heading: Signature and Lorentzian Metrics
sections.body:
Dropping positive-definiteness while keeping non-degeneracy gives a pseudo-Riemannian metric, classified by its signature. The case of signature \((-,+,+,+)\) is Lorentzian, and is the setting of relativity. Flat spacetime carries the Minkowski metric

\[ ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 \]

where the minus sign separates timelike from spacelike directions and makes the light cone a geometric object rather than a convention. Vectors of zero length are no longer only the zero vector — they are the null directions light travels along.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.body:
In general relativity the metric of spacetime is the gravitational field; Einstein’s field equations, which in geometrised units \(G=c=1\) read \(G_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi T_{\mu\nu}\), constrain its curvature in terms of the matter present, and free particles follow geodesics. Satellite navigation applies this at engineering scale: orbital clocks are corrected for the difference between their metric and ours, and neglecting it would accumulate positional error of several kilometres a day.

Beyond physics, metrics appear wherever a curved parameter space needs measuring — in information geometry the Fisher information matrix is a metric on a family of probability distributions, and in shape analysis and machine learning geodesic distance replaces straight-line distance on manifolds of data.

references: do Carmo, M.P. Riemannian Geometry. Birkhäuser, 1992.
Lee, J.M. Introduction to Riemannian Manifolds, 2nd ed. Springer, 2018.
O’Neill, B. Semi-Riemannian Geometry with Applications to Relativity. Academic Press, 1983.
Misner, C.W., Thorne, K.S. and Wheeler, J.A. Gravitation. W.H. Freeman, 1973.

articles.title: Sets
articles.author: Dr. J. Alcaraz
articles.abstract: A set is a collection of distinct objects considered as a single object, determined entirely by which things belong to it.

sections.heading: Intuition
sections.body: A set is specified by its members and nothing else — not by order, not by repetition, not by how it was described. \(\{1,2,3\}\), \(\{3,1,2\}\) and \(\{1,1,2,3\}\) all denote the same set. Two different descriptions can name the same set: \(\{x \in \mathbb{N} : x^2 = 4\}\) and \(\{2\}\) are equal.

sections.heading: Formal definition
sections.body:
Membership, written \(x \in A\), is taken as primitive rather than defined. Sets are then pinned down by the axiom of extensionality:

\[ A = B \iff \forall x\,(x \in A \iff x \in B) \]

This is a definition of equality, not a theorem. Naive comprehension — the assumption that any property defines a set — is inconsistent: taking \(R = \{x : x \notin x\}\) gives \(R \in R \iff R \notin R\), which is Russell's paradox. Modern treatments therefore use an axiom system such as ZFC, in which comprehension is restricted to selecting a subset of a set that already exists.

sections.heading: Notation
sections.body:
\(x \in A\) membership; \(A \subseteq B\) inclusion, meaning every element of \(A\) lies in \(B\); \(A \subsetneq B\) proper inclusion; \(\varnothing\) the empty set; \(A \cup B\), \(A \cap B\), \(A \setminus B\) union, intersection, difference; \(\mathcal{P}(A)\) the power set, whose elements are the subsets of \(A\); \(|A|\) cardinality; \(A \times B = \{(a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B\}\) the Cartesian product.

The standard number sets are \(\mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{Z}\), \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathbb{C}\). Note that \(\subset\) is used by some authors for proper inclusion and by others for inclusion generally; \(\subseteq\) and \(\subsetneq\) are unambiguous and are used throughout this site.

sections.heading: Key properties
sections.body:
For all sets \(A, B, C\):

\[ A \cup B = B \cup A, \qquad A \cap B = B \cap A \]

\[ A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C) \]

and, relative to a universe \(U\), De Morgan's laws

\[ (A \cup B)^{c} = A^{c} \cap B^{c}, \qquad (A \cap B)^{c} = A^{c} \cup B^{c} \]

For a finite set, \(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|}\) and \(|A \times B| = |A|\cdot|B|\). Both require finiteness as stated; the first generalises to Cantor's theorem below.

sections.heading: Theorem (Cantor)
sections.body:
Statement. For every set \(A\) there is no surjection \(A \to \mathcal{P}(A)\); in particular \(|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|\).

Proof. Let \(f : A \to \mathcal{P}(A)\) be any function and put \(D = \{a \in A : a \notin f(a)\}\). If \(D = f(a_0)\) for some \(a_0 \in A\), then \(a_0 \in D \iff a_0 \notin f(a_0) = D\), a contradiction. So \(D\) is not in the image and \(f\) is not surjective. \(\blacksquare\)

This is a complete proof, not a sketch, and it is the reason there is no largest cardinality.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
Let \(A = \{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(B = \{3,4,5\}\).

\(A \cup B = \{1,2,3,4,5\}\), so \(|A \cup B| = 5\).
\(A \cap B = \{3,4\}\), so \(|A \cap B| = 2\).
\(A \setminus B = \{1,2\}\) and \(B \setminus A = \{5\}\) — the difference is not symmetric.
\(|A \times B| = 4 \times 3 = 12\).
\(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{4} = 16\).

Inclusion–exclusion checks out: \(|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| = 4 + 3 - 2 = 5\).

sections.heading: Common misconception
sections.body:
\(\varnothing\) and \(\{\varnothing\}\) are different sets: the first has no elements, the second has exactly one, namely \(\varnothing\). So \(|\varnothing| = 0\) but \(|\{\varnothing\}| = 1\).

Equally common is conflating \(\in\) with \(\subseteq\). For \(A = \{1,2\}\) we have \(1 \in A\) and \(\{1\} \subseteq A\), but \(1 \subseteq A\) is not well formed and \(\{1\} \in A\) is false.

references: Halmos, P.R. Naive Set Theory. Van Nostrand, 1960.
Enderton, H.B. Elements of Set Theory. Academic Press, 1977.

articles.title: Functions
articles.author: Dr. J. Alcaraz
articles.abstract: A function f: A → B assigns to each element of a domain A exactly one element of a codomain B.

sections.heading: Intuition
sections.body: A function is a rule that is total and deterministic: every input in the domain gets an output, and never more than one. The familiar vertical line test is exactly this condition drawn in the plane for a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

sections.heading: Formal definition
sections.body:
A function \(f : A \to B\) is a subset \(f \subseteq A \times B\) such that for every \(a \in A\) there is exactly one \(b \in B\) with \((a,b) \in f\); that \(b\) is written \(f(a)\).

Defining a function as a set of ordered pairs means that the domain and codomain are part of the data. \(g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},\ g(x)=x^2\) and \(h : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty),\ h(x)=x^2\) are different functions even though the formula is the same, and they have different properties.

sections.heading: Notation
sections.body: \(f : A \to B\) declares the function; \(A = \operatorname{dom} f\) is the domain and \(B\) the codomain. The image is \(f(A) = \{f(a) : a \in A\} \subseteq B\). Composition is \((g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))\), defined when the codomain of \(f\) is contained in the domain of \(g\). The identity on \(A\) is \(\mathrm{id}_A\).

sections.heading: Key properties
sections.body:
\(f\) is injective if \(f(x)=f(y) \Rightarrow x=y\); surjective if \(f(A) = B\); bijective if both.

Composition is associative, \((h \circ g)\circ f = h \circ (g \circ f)\), but not commutative in general.

A two-sided inverse exists if and only if \(f\) is a bijection. The two halves are separate: \(f\) has a left inverse if and only if it is injective, and a right inverse if and only if it is surjective (the latter using the axiom of choice in general).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
Take \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = 2x+1\) and \(g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},\ g(x) = x^2\).

\((f \circ g)(3) = f(9) = 2(9)+1 = 19\), while \((g \circ f)(3) = g(7) = 49\). The two orders disagree, which is the general situation.

\(f\) is a bijection: solving \(y = 2x+1\) gives the inverse \(f^{-1}(y) = \tfrac{y-1}{2}\), and \(f^{-1}(f(x)) = \tfrac{(2x+1)-1}{2} = x\).

\(g\) is neither injective (\(g(-2)=g(2)=4\)) nor surjective onto \(\mathbb{R}\) (nothing maps to \(-1\)). Restricting the domain and codomain to \([0,\infty)\) makes it a bijection with inverse \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) — which is why \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x|\) rather than \(x\).

sections.heading: Common misconception
sections.body:
The codomain is not the image. \(g : \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R},\ g(x)=x^2\) has codomain \(\mathbb{R}\) but image \([0,\infty)\), and surjectivity is a statement about the codomain you declared. Saying "the range of \(g\) is \(\mathbb{R}\)" is simply false.

Relatedly, \(f^{-1}\) is used for two different things: the inverse function, which needs \(f\) to be a bijection, and the preimage \(f^{-1}(S) = \{a : f(a) \in S\}\), which is always defined.

references: Halmos, P.R. Naive Set Theory. Van Nostrand, 1960.
Velleman, D.J. How to Prove It: A Structured Approach, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press, 2006.

articles.title: Limits
articles.author: Dr. E. Marchetti
articles.abstract: The limit of f at a is the value L that f(x) approaches as x approaches a, made precise by the requirement that f(x) can be forced within any tolerance of L by taking x close enough to a.

sections.heading: Intuition
sections.body: A limit describes what the outputs do near a point, deliberately ignoring what happens at it. This is what makes the difference quotient of a derivative meaningful: the quotient is undefined at \(h=0\), and the limit is what supplies the missing value.

sections.heading: Formal definition
sections.body:
Let \(f\) be defined on a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\). Then \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) means:

\[ \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists \delta > 0 : \ 0 < |x-a| < \delta \implies |f(x)-L| < \varepsilon \]

The condition \(0 < |x-a|\) excludes \(x = a\) itself, so \(f\) need not be defined at \(a\) and its value there is irrelevant. The order of quantifiers matters: \(\delta\) is chosen after \(\varepsilon\) and may depend on it.

sections.heading: Notation
sections.body: \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\); one-sided limits \(\lim_{x \to a^{-}}\) and \(\lim_{x \to a^{+}}\); \(\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L\) for behaviour at infinity. Writing \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = \infty\) asserts unbounded growth; it records a mode of divergence rather than a real value.

sections.heading: Key properties
sections.body:
A limit, if it exists, is unique. If \(\lim_{x\to a} f = L\) and \(\lim_{x\to a} g = M\), both finite, then

\[ \lim_{x\to a}(f+g) = L+M, \qquad \lim_{x\to a}(fg) = LM, \qquad \lim_{x\to a}\frac{f}{g} = \frac{L}{M}\ \ \text{provided } M \neq 0 \]

The two-sided limit exists if and only if both one-sided limits exist and agree.

Squeeze theorem. If \(g(x) \le f(x) \le h(x)\) on a punctured neighbourhood of \(a\) and \(\lim_{x\to a} g = \lim_{x\to a} h = L\), then \(\lim_{x\to a} f = L\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
Algebraic. Evaluate \(\lim_{x \to 2} \dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}\). Substitution gives \(0/0\), which is not a value but a signal that the factor \(x-2\) is common. Factoring, \(\dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x+2\) for every \(x \neq 2\), and since the limit ignores \(x=2\) the answer is \(2+2 = 4\).

From the definition. Show \(\lim_{x \to 3}(2x+1) = 7\). Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), note \(|(2x+1)-7| = 2|x-3|\). Choosing \(\delta = \varepsilon/2\), whenever \(0 < |x-3| < \delta\) we get \(|(2x+1)-7| = 2|x-3| < 2\delta = \varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, the limit is \(7\).

sections.heading: Common misconception
sections.body:
\(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)\) is not a definition — it is precisely the definition of continuity at \(a\), and it fails in general. The worked example above has a limit of \(4\) at a point where the function has no value at all.

Similarly, \(0/0\) is not a number and not "equal to 1". It is an indeterminate form: it records that the limit is not settled by substitution and says nothing about the answer, which may be any real number, \(\pm\infty\), or nonexistent.

references: Rudin, W. Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill, 1976.
Abbott, S. Understanding Analysis, 2nd ed. Springer, 2015.
OpenStax. Calculus Volume 1, Chapter 2. openstax.org, 2016.

articles.title: Derivatives
articles.author: Dr. E. Marchetti
articles.abstract: The derivative of f at a is the limit of its difference quotients at a, when that limit exists; it is the instantaneous rate of change of f and the slope of the tangent line at that point.

sections.heading: Intuition
sections.body: Average rate of change over an interval is rise over run. Shrinking the interval to nothing turns the secant line into the tangent line, and the average rate into an instantaneous one. The limit is doing essential work: the quotient is literally \(0/0\) at \(h=0\).

sections.heading: Formal definition
sections.body:
\(f\) is differentiable at an interior point \(a\) of its domain if

\[ f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \]

exists and is finite. Equivalently \(f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}\). A function is differentiable on an open interval if it is differentiable at each of its points.

sections.heading: Notation
sections.body: Lagrange \(f'(x)\); Leibniz \(\dfrac{df}{dx}\) or \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\); operator \(D f\); Newton \(\dot{x}\) for a time derivative. Higher derivatives: \(f''\), \(f^{(n)}\), \(\dfrac{d^n f}{dx^n}\). Evaluation at a point is written \(\left.\dfrac{df}{dx}\right|_{x=a}\).

sections.heading: Key properties
sections.body:
Differentiability at \(a\) implies continuity at \(a\). The converse is false: \(f(x)=|x|\) is continuous at \(0\) but the one-sided difference quotients tend to \(-1\) and \(+1\), so no derivative exists there.

For differentiable \(u, v\):

\[ (u+v)' = u'+v', \qquad (uv)' = u'v + uv' \]

\[ \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)' = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}} \ \ \text{where } v \neq 0, \qquad (g \circ f)'(x) = g'(f(x))\,f'(x) \]

sections.heading: Theorem (Mean Value Theorem)
sections.body:
Statement. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then there exists \(c \in (a,b)\) with

\[ f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \]

Proof sketch. Subtract the secant line from \(f\) to obtain a function vanishing at both endpoints, then apply Rolle's theorem, which itself follows from the extreme value theorem plus the vanishing of the derivative at an interior extremum. This is a sketch, not a proof: the omitted steps are Rolle's theorem and the extreme value theorem.

Both hypotheses are needed. \(f(x)=|x|\) on \([-1,1]\) is continuous but not differentiable at \(0\), and no \(c\) satisfies the conclusion, since \(f'\) takes only the values \(\pm 1\) while the secant slope is \(0\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
From the definition. For \(f(x)=x^{2}\),

\[ \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} = \frac{(a+h)^2 - a^2}{h} = \frac{2ah + h^2}{h} = 2a + h \quad (h \neq 0) \]

so \(f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0}(2a+h) = 2a\).

By the rules. For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 4x\), term by term \(f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 4\). At \(x = 2\), \(f'(2) = 3(4) - 4 = 8\).

Setting \(f'(x)=0\) gives \(x = \pm\sqrt{4/3} = \pm 2/\sqrt{3} \approx \pm 1.1547\), the two turning points visible in the figure. Note that \(f'(c)=0\) is necessary but not sufficient for a local extremum: \(x^{3}\) has \(f'(0)=0\) and no extremum at \(0\).

sections.heading: Common misconception
sections.body:
Continuity does not imply differentiability. Beyond \(|x|\), Weierstrass constructed functions continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) and differentiable nowhere.

\(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) is a single symbol denoting a limit, not a quotient of two quantities \(dy\) and \(dx\). The chain rule is not cancellation of differentials, even though the notation is chosen to make it look that way.

references: Spivak, M. Calculus, 4th ed. Publish or Perish, 2008.
Rudin, W. Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill, 1976.
MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.01 Single Variable Calculus. ocw.mit.edu.
